notes.b: Health-related fitness is the set of fitness components that matter for staying healthy as well as for sport. The first is cardio-respiratory endurance, which is about how well your body keeps supplying oxygen to working muscles.
points: Definition: the ability of the heart, lungs and blood vessels to take in, transport and use oxygen to sustain whole-body activity over a long period. It is also called aerobic fitness or stamina.

It depends on the aerobic energy system (the way the body releases energy from fuel using oxygen), which is why oxygen delivery by the heart, lungs and blood vessels decides how long you can keep going.
It is important in distance running, distance swimming, soccer and Gaelic football, because players in these activities are active for over an hour.
Health benefit: it lowers the risk of heart disease, stroke and high blood pressure.
notes.tip: Define it as whole-body: heart, lungs and blood vessels taking in, transporting and using oxygen over a long period. Do not define it using muscular endurance, which is local to one muscle group.

notes.b: Muscular endurance sounds like cardio-respiratory endurance but is a different component. It is about how long one muscle or muscle group can keep working, not the whole body.
points: Definition: the ability of a muscle or muscle group to perform repeated contractions (the tightening of a muscle as it produces force) over a period of time without tiring.
It is local to a muscle group, whereas cardio-respiratory endurance involves the whole body. This is the key distinction to state when comparing them.

It matters for the legs of a rower or cyclist, the arms in repeated tackles, and the core and legs of a dancer holding positions through a routine, because each of these muscle groups must keep working over and over.
Health benefit: it makes everyday tasks such as climbing stairs and carrying shopping easier and supports good posture.
notes.tip: Keep the two endurances separate: muscular endurance is local to a muscle group, cardio-respiratory endurance is the whole body. Do not use one to define the other.

notes.b: Strength is the force a muscle can produce. It comes in several forms depending on how fast, how often and whether the body moves while the force is applied.
points: Definition: the maximum force a muscle or muscle group can exert against a resistance in a single contraction.
Maximal strength is the greatest force you can produce in one all-out effort, such as pushing in a rugby scrum (the forwards driving against the opposing pack).
Explosive (elastic) strength is force applied quickly, such as a jump take-off. It is the basis of power, so it is the link to the next subsection.
Strength endurance is repeated sub-maximal force (below your maximum, so it can be repeated) over time, such as a rower's stroke.
Static strength is used without movement, such as holding a position on the rings (the hanging gymnastics apparatus). Dynamic strength is used with movement, such as lifting a weight.
In terms of training intensity, strength is built with heavy loads and few repetitions, while muscular endurance is built with lighter loads and many repetitions.
Health benefit: it protects joints, supports bone density and makes daily lifting safer.
notes.tip: When asked to describe the difference between training for muscular endurance and for strength in terms of intensity, say heavy loads and few repetitions for strength, lighter loads and many repetitions for muscular endurance. Power is not a form of strength in the specification's list; mention explosive strength only as the link.

notes.b: Flexibility is about how far your joints can move. A joint is where two bones meet, so more range at the joints means the body can reach and stretch further.
points: Definition: the range of movement possible at a joint or series of joints.
Static flexibility is the range a joint can reach and hold at rest, such as a held split.
Dynamic flexibility is the range used during movement, such as a hurdler's lead leg (the first leg to go over the hurdle) or a high kick in dance.
It is important in gymnastics, dance, hurdles, goalkeeping and tennis, where the body must stretch to reach the ball.
Benefits: better technique through a full range of movement, less risk of muscle strains (muscles overstretched or torn), and easier everyday movement.
notes.tip: Be ready to define flexibility and to say why it matters for a tennis player: the body must stretch to reach the ball. Reduced injury risk is also a point to make.

notes.b: Body composition looks at what the body is made of rather than how much it weighs. It is the last of the five health-related fitness components.
points: Definition: the relative proportions of fat mass and lean (fat-free) mass (muscle, bone and organs) in the body, usually given as a body-fat percentage (the share of total body weight that is fat).
It is not the same as body weight: two people of the same weight can have very different body composition, because one may carry more fat and the other more muscle.
Different activities favour different compositions: a low body-fat percentage suits distance running, while more lean mass suits a rugby forward.
Somatotypes (body-shape types) are ectomorph (lean and linear), mesomorph (muscular) and endomorph (rounder, with more fat). Most people are a mix.
Health benefit: a healthy body-fat percentage lowers the risk of type 2 diabetes (a condition affecting how the body handles blood sugar), heart disease and joint problems.
notes.tip: Define body composition as the proportions of fat mass and lean mass, usually as body-fat percentage. Do not equate it with body weight or BMI.

factCards.definition: Cardio-respiratory endurance is whole-body and relies on the heart and lungs; muscular endurance is local to one muscle group.

factCards.term: Training intensity: strength versus muscular endurance
factCards.definition: Strength: heavy loads, few repetitions. Muscular endurance: lighter loads, many repetitions.

factCards.term: Why flexibility matters for a tennis player
factCards.definition: A full range at the shoulder gives a powerful serve and the reach to stretch for wide balls, and reduces the risk of strains.

questions.prompt: Define the five components of health-related fitness.
questions.model: 1. Cardio-respiratory endurance: the ability of the heart, lungs and blood vessels to take in, transport and use oxygen to sustain whole-body activity over a long period, such as running a 10 km race. 2. Muscular endurance: the ability of a muscle or muscle group to perform repeated contractions over time without tiring, such as a rower's legs. 3. Strength: the maximum force a muscle or muscle group can exert against a resistance in one contraction, such as pushing in a scrum. 4. Flexibility: the range of movement possible at a joint, such as a gymnast's split. 5. Body composition: the relative proportions of fat mass and lean mass in the body, usually given as a body-fat percentage.

questions.prompt: Define flexibility and explain why it is important in a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Flexibility is the range of movement possible at a joint or series of joints. In hurdling, the lead leg must lift high and straight and the trail leg must rotate out to the side to clear each hurdle without raising the body's centre of mass, which needs a wide range at the hip. Good flexibility also reduces the risk of hamstring strains from the long stride.
